# chilling-effects-skeptic-trail
- **URL:** https://scholarship.law.wm.edu/facpubs/879/ (Schauer, landing only; PDF gated) · https://scholarship.law.wm.edu/wmlr/vol54/iss5/4/ (Kendrick; full PDF read via wmlawreview.org mirror) · https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3855619 (Penney 2022; SSRN blocked, abstract verified via https://digitalcommons.schulichlaw.dal.ca/scholarly_works/1799/) · **Accessed:** 2026-08-25 · **For:** v1→v2 response round, honestly characterizing the skeptical empirical literature on chilling effects
- **What it establishes:** The skeptical line inside the chilling-effects literature itself, with exact citations. (1) Frederick Schauer, *Fear, Risk and the First Amendment: Unraveling the "Chilling Effect,"* 58 B.U. L. Rev. 685 (1978) — the doctrine's founding theorist conceded that its empirical/behavioral assumptions are "most likely unprovable," at p. 730. Full text unreachable (repository PDF 403-blocked); the phrase and pincite are corroborated by two independent secondary quotations: Penney 2016 (31 Berkeley Tech. L.J. at 121 & n.12: "admitted in 1978 that its empirical assumptions about human behavior were 'most likely unprovable'") and Bedi, *The Myth of the Chilling Effect*, 35 Harv. J.L. & Tech. 267, 271 & n.10 (2021) ("A leading scholar once commented that the human behaviors that underly the chilling effect are 'most likely unprovable.'"). The two-word-phrase quotation is safe; the full surrounding sentence is NOT verified (search-level; verify before print quotation beyond the phrase itself). Bedi also preserves Schauer's definition verbatim: chilling occurs "when individuals seeking to engage in activity protected by the [F]irst [A]mendment are deterred from so doing by governmental regulation not specifically directed at that protected activity" (Schauer at 693, via Bedi n.19) and "The very essence of a chilling effect is an act of deterrence" (Schauer at 689, via Bedi n.21) — both secondary-verified. (2) Leslie Kendrick, *Speech, Intent, and the Chilling Effect*, 54 Wm. & Mary L. Rev. 1633 (2013) — FULL TEXT VERIFIED. Her "flimsy" is a characterization of the Justices' evidentiary basis, not a blanket denial: "Dissents and majorities routinely criticize each other for the flimsy empirical basis of their assessments of chilling" (p. 1656). Surrounding argument: the Court "has relied on little more than crude empirical speculation" (p. 1656); the chilling effect's influence "is founded on little more than a collection of unsubstantiated empirical judgments" (p. 1657); "both the detection of a problem and the imposition of a remedy involve intractable empirical difficulties" (p. 1638). Crucially she also writes: "This is not to say that the chilling effect is not a real phenomenon. Nor is it to say that the chilling effect should play no role in the development of First Amendment rules" (p. 1638). (3) Jonathon Penney, *Understanding Chilling Effects*, 106 Minn. L. Rev. 1451 (2022) (SSRN id 3855619) — Penney's own later concession, VERIFIED VERBATIM from the publisher-deposited abstract: "I argue that conventional theories, based on fear of legal or privacy harm, are narrow, empirically weak, cannot predict or explain chilling effects in a range of different contexts, and neglect its productive dimensions." NOTE the exact wording is "narrow, empirically weak" (a comma list), not "narrow and empirically weak" — quote accordingly. His reconstruction: "chilling effects are best understood as a form of social conformity" arising "out of contexts of ambiguity and uncertainty." (4) Bonus skeptic datum (full text read): Bedi's own empirical study of online restaurant reviews found "the chilling effect created little to no impact on the content of the message; at most, it slightly altered the specific style or tone used" (35 Harv. J.L. & Tech. at ~271–72).
- **Key passages:** Schauer: "most likely unprovable" (58 B.U. L. Rev. at 730) (phrase verified via two independent secondary quotations; full sentence search-level; verify before print quotation). Kendrick: "Dissents and majorities routinely criticize each other for the flimsy empirical basis of their assessments of chilling." (54 Wm. & Mary L. Rev. at 1656, verified from full text). Kendrick: "founded on little more than a collection of unsubstantiated empirical judgments" (id. at 1657, verified). Kendrick's caveat: "This is not to say that the chilling effect is not a real phenomenon." (id. at 1638, verified). Penney 2022 abstract: "conventional theories, based on fear of legal or privacy harm, are narrow, empirically weak, cannot predict or explain chilling effects in a range of different contexts" (verified verbatim, publisher abstract).
- **Reliability:** Kendrick and Bedi: primary full texts, verified. Schauer: secondary corroboration only (two independent scholarly quotations agreeing on wording and pincite) — high confidence in the phrase, but flag it. Penney 2022 abstract: publisher/author-deposited repository copy, effectively primary. All are academic sources with no relevant institutional bias; note Penney has a stake in chilling effects being real (he is the field's leading empiricist), which makes his "empirically weak" concession *more* probative, not less.
- **Relevance to this project:** Supports the essay's obligation to characterize the empirical literature honestly: the doctrine's founder (Schauer 1978), its sharpest doctrinal critic (Kendrick 2013), and its leading empiricist (Penney 2022) all concede the conventional fear-based empirical case is thin. Use Kendrick precisely — her "flimsy" targets the *courts'* evidentiary practice, and she expressly does not deny the phenomenon; misquoting her as denying chilling effects would be a fact-check failure. Pairs with penney-wikipedia-chilling-2016 (the behavioral evidence that post-dates Schauer's and Kendrick's complaints) and frames the essay's move: the right response to weak fear-based accounts is better behavioral evidence plus Penney's conformity theory, not abandonment of the claim.
